templates.title: User edits and pipeline syncs on the same object: current values and the share held by edits
templates.subtopic: latest-wins resolution with tie rules, as-of filtering, conditional aggregation

sections.scenario: A manufacturer's operations team works in an operational application built on an ontology of objects: machines, work orders, suppliers, shipments. Pipelines sync property values from the source systems on a schedule, and planners also edit properties directly in the application. Both kinds of write land in one log. The team wants to know, per object type, how much of what people currently see comes from user edits rather than from the systems of record: a high share means the application and the sources have drifted apart.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns object_type, objects, properties, edit_held, edit_share, one row per object type that has at least one current property value, ordered by object_type. Report the state as of {{as_of}} (the report instant): only writes with written_at <= that instant exist, and an object whose deleted_at is at or before it is left out entirely. {{delete_rule}} The current value of a property of an object comes from its winning write: the latest written_at wins, and at an equal written_at an edit beats a sync (this exercise's rule). If two writes of the same source share an instant, the higher write_id wins. {{tie_rule}} write_id is assigned on arrival, so it is not in written_at order. A write whose value is NULL clears the property: if it wins, the property has no current value and is not counted. {{null_rule}} properties counts the (object, property) pairs with a current value; edit_held counts those whose winning write is an edit; objects counts the objects of the type with at least one current value; edit_share is edit_held / properties rounded to 4 decimal places.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The report instant is inclusive for writes and for deletions. The sample has {{writes}} writes; assume billions of property writes across tens of millions of objects in production.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical object types, properties, values and volumes. The resolution rule (latest wins, ties to the edit) is this exercise's model; real platforms let each object type configure how user edits and source updates combine, so check current docs. written_at is when the write took effect.
sections.criteria: Filters by the report instant before choosing a winner and removes deleted objects; latest written_at wins, edits win ties, then the higher write_id; the NULL test comes after ranking; counts per type with a numeric, rounded share; deterministic order; can discuss as-of history and how to keep a resent snapshot from overriding edits.

clarifications.q: If a sync arrives after a user edit, does the edit survive?
clarifications.a: No. The latest write wins whatever its source; the edit wins only a tie at the same instant.

clarifications.q: What does a NULL value mean?
clarifications.a: The property was cleared. A winning NULL leaves no current value; an older non-NULL value does not come back.

clarifications.q: Is write_id the order of the writes?
clarifications.a: No. It is the order writes reached the log. Order by written_at; write_id only breaks a tie between two writes of the same source at the same instant, and the higher one wins.

clarifications.q: Is a write exactly at the report instant included?
clarifications.a: Yes. And an object deleted exactly at the report instant is gone.

clarifications.q: Does an object type with no current values appear?
clarifications.a: No. Only types with at least one current value.

hints: Rank the writes of each (object_id, property) with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY object_id, property ORDER BY written_at DESC, (source = 'edit') DESC, write_id DESC) and keep rank 1.
Apply the report-instant filter before ranking and the NULL test after ranking. Swapping either one changes the answer.
COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE source = 'edit'), and cast to numeric before dividing.
followups: Product wants the value a user saw on any past date, for any object. How do you store and query "value as of t" over billions of writes so it stays cheap?

After an outage a source system resends yesterday's full snapshot, and the pipeline stamps every row with the resend time. What happens to the user edits made in between, and how would you change the model so a resend cannot override them?
Some properties must never be edited by users and others should always prefer the edit. How do you model per-property resolution rules and keep this report correct?
The share must update within a minute of each write across 50 million objects. How do you maintain it incrementally, including when a winning write is a NULL that clears a value?

rules.ask: If you take MAX(written_at) per property and join back to the writes, how many rows come back when an edit and a sync share that instant?
Your ORDER BY decides every tie. Read it back: which write wins when two syncs share an instant, and why?
Is your NULL test applied before or after you pick the winner? Show an input where the order matters.
write_id is the arrival order. Why is ordering by it alone wrong here, and when is it the right tie-breaker?
If the sync pipeline upserted current values instead of appending writes, what could this report no longer tell you?

templates.title: Reads after expiry: restricted datasets read after the reader's purpose-based grant had ended
templates.subtopic: interval coverage with LEFT JOIN, NULL-aware LEAST, three-way classification

sections.scenario: A utility's data platform is moving to a stricter access model (this exercise's model): some datasets carry a restrictive marking, and reading one needs a grant for that user, that dataset and a stated purpose, with an expiry. Renewals are issued as new grants. Before the new rules are enforced, the governance team replays the read log against the grant history in a dry run, to see how many reads the rules would have flagged and why: because a grant had lapsed, or because there never was one.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns dataset_id, read_month, restricted_reads, after_expiry, never_granted, max_hours_late, one row per dataset and UTC month with at least one counted read, ordered by dataset_id, read_month. A read counts only when its dataset was restricted at the time: marking is not NULL and marked_since <= read_at. {{marked_rule}} A grant matches a read when it has the same user_id, dataset_id and purpose. {{purpose_rule}} A matching grant covers the read when granted_at <= read_at < end, where end is expires_at, or revoked_at if that is earlier. {{revoke_rule}} Renewals are separate grant rows; any covering grant is enough. Each counted read is exactly one of: covered; after expiry: not covered, but at least one matching grant had granted_at <= read_at (so every such grant had ended); never granted: no matching grant had started. restricted_reads counts all counted reads. read_month is the first day of the read's UTC month, as a DATE. max_hours_late is, over the month's after-expiry reads, the largest number of hours from the latest end among the read's matching started grants to the read, rounded to 1 decimal place; NULL when the month has none.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). A read exactly at a grant's end is not covered by it; a read exactly at granted_at is. The sample has {{reads}} reads and {{grants}} grants; assume billions of reads a month in production.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical datasets, markings, purposes and pseudonymous user ids. The marking, purpose and expiry rules are this exercise's model of purpose-based access, not a description of how any product enforces access; check current docs. All timestamps are UTC.
sections.criteria: Counts only reads of datasets marked at the time; matches on user, dataset and purpose; half-open coverage where any grant is enough; the end as the earlier of expiry and revocation; a LEFT JOIN that keeps never-granted reads; hours from the latest end; UTC months as dates; deterministic order; can explain how to run the check incrementally.

clarifications.q: A grant expired and was renewed two days later. What about a read in between?
clarifications.a: After expiry. A read is covered only if some grant covers that instant.

clarifications.q: The renewal was issued before the old grant expired.
clarifications.a: Then they overlap, and a read in the overlap or after the old expiry (but inside the renewal) is covered.

clarifications.q: Does a grant for another purpose cover the read?
clarifications.a: No. The purpose is part of the match.

clarifications.q: Which end do I measure the hours from?
clarifications.a: The latest end among the matching grants that had started by the read.

clarifications.q: What if a revocation was recorded after the grant had already expired?
clarifications.a: The end is the earlier of the two, so it changes nothing.

clarifications.q: Reads of datasets that are not marked?
clarifications.a: Not counted, and they produce no rows.

hints: LEFT JOIN each counted read to its matching grants, with granted_at <= read_at in the join condition, so reads with no started grant survive; then aggregate per read.
Per read you need three things: how many matching grants had started, whether any covers it (bool_or), and the latest end (MAX).
In PostgreSQL LEAST(expires_at, revoked_at) ignores a NULL argument. COALESCE(revoked_at, expires_at) is not the same thing.
followups: The review wants every after-expiry read listed with the approver of the grant that lapsed last. How do you produce it without duplicating reads that had several expired grants?
The read log is billions of rows a month. How would you compute this incrementally, and which sort order or index makes the per-read grant lookup cheap?
In this exercise's model markings are inherited by derived datasets. How would the query change if a derived dataset is restricted whenever any of its inputs is?
Before enforcement starts, how would you present these numbers to dataset owners so they lead to fixes rather than blame?

rules.ask: What happens to a read whose user never had a grant on that dataset? Where does it appear in your output?
COALESCE(revoked_at, expires_at) and LEAST(expires_at, revoked_at) differ for one kind of grant. Which kind, and which does the specification want?
BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends. Which read does that misclassify here?
You compare each grant with the next one. What happens when three grants overlap and the middle one ends last?
An EXISTS test classifies the read. How do you also get the hours late without a second pass over the grants?

templates.title: First-pass yield per production line and shift, with night shifts that cross midnight
templates.subtopic: first and last per group, shift calendars, time zones

sections.scenario: A manufacturer integrates end-of-line test results from its plants into one operational view. Every unit is tested; failures are reworked and retested, sometimes at a station on another line. Plant managers compare lines and shifts by first-pass yield, the share of units that pass their first test, and want retests counted by how they finally ended. Shifts run 06:00–14:00 (day), 14:00–22:00 (swing) and 22:00–06:00 (night) in plant local time, and a night shift belongs to the date it started.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns line_id, shift_date, shift, units, first_pass, retested, final_pass, fpy, one row per line, shift date and shift with at least one unit, ordered by line_id, shift_date, shift. A unit's attempts are its tests with result 'pass' or 'fail', ordered by tested_at, then test_id; a 'void' test is an aborted run and is not an attempt. {{void_rule}} A unit with no attempts is not counted. Each unit is counted once, under the line, shift date and shift of its first attempt, wherever its later attempts happened. first_pass counts units whose first attempt passed; retested counts units with more than one attempt; final_pass counts units whose last attempt passed; fpy is first_pass / units rounded to 4 decimal places. {{tz_rule}} The shifts are day [06:00, 14:00), swing [14:00, 22:00) and night [22:00, 06:00); a test before 06:00 belongs to the night shift of the previous date.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). 06:00:00 opens the day shift, 14:00:00 the swing shift and 22:00:00 the night shift. test_id is the upload order, not the test order. The sample has {{tests}} test records.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical lines, serial numbers and results. The shift pattern and the yield definitions are this exercise's. Retests can happen on a rework station attached to another line.
sections.criteria: Ignores voids before ordering attempts; first and last attempt by tested_at then test_id; one row per unit, placed by its first attempt; correct local shift and shift date across midnight; final outcome from the last attempt; numeric, rounded yield; deterministic order; can discuss late data and daylight saving changes.

clarifications.q: A unit failed on one line and was retested on another. Which line gets it?
clarifications.a: The line of its first attempt.

clarifications.q: A unit passed, was sent back for a re-test and failed.
clarifications.a: Its final outcome is fail: the last attempt decides. It still counts as a first pass.

clarifications.q: Two attempts of a unit have the same tested_at.
clarifications.a: The lower test_id came first.

clarifications.q: Does a void count as a failed first attempt?
clarifications.a: No. Voids are ignored entirely.

clarifications.q: Which shift is a test at 02:00 on 16 September?
clarifications.a: The night shift of 15 September.

hints: ROW_NUMBER() per unit in both directions gives the first and the last attempt; COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY unit_serial) gives the number of attempts.
Remove voids in WHERE, before the window functions.
Convert to plant local time first (tested_at AT TIME ZONE '…' gives a local timestamp). Subtracting 6 hours and casting to date gives the shift date of every shift.
followups: Managers also want rolled throughput yield across three test stations in sequence. How does it differ from first-pass yield, and what extra data does it need?
A plant changes clocks for daylight saving time during a night shift. How long is that shift, and what should the report show for it?
Results from some testers arrive up to two days late. When is a shift's yield final, and how do you correct one that was already published?
One line's yield jumps from 0.82 to 0.97 overnight. What would you check in the data before believing it?

rules.ask: Which shift_date does your query give a test at 02:30 local time, and which should it be?
MIN(tested_at) finds the first time. How do you get that attempt's result and line, and what if two attempts share it?
Shifts are in plant local time. At a plant 5½ hours ahead of UTC, which shift does a test at 03:00 UTC belong to?
A unit passed and then failed a re-test. What does your final_pass say for it, and what should it say?
Where are voids removed in your query? What changes for a unit whose first test was void?

templates.title: Pipeline cycles: the groups of datasets that depend on each other
templates.subtopic: strongly connected components, iterative depth-first search (O(V + E) versus a search from every dataset, O(V·(V + E)))

sections.scenario: An enterprise data platform builds datasets from other datasets: each dataset declares the inputs its transform reads. A build runs inputs before the datasets that read them, which is impossible when datasets depend on each other in a cycle, usually by accident (a cleaned table that reads a report built from it). Before the nightly build, a check lists every such group so their owners can break them.
sections.problem: Implement pipeline_cycles(inputs). inputs maps each declared dataset to the list of datasets it reads. An input that is not a key is a raw source, which reads nothing. Return every cycle group: a largest set of two or more datasets in which each one depends, directly or through other datasets, on every other one; or a single dataset that lists itself as an input. Each group is a list sorted ascending, and the groups are sorted by their first element. Return [] when there are none. {{self_rule}} {{depth_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 datasets and 400 000 declared inputs. Expected O(V + E) time and memory. Do not assume the search depth fits Python's default recursion limit.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical dataset names and sizes. The order of keys and of inputs carries no meaning, and an input can be listed twice.
sections.criteria: Recognises strongly connected components; one linear pass (Tarjan or Kosaraju) that does not depend on the recursion limit; raw sources, self-loops and duplicate inputs handled; groups and members sorted as specified; can explain why reachability from every dataset is quadratic and how the condensation DAG supports build scheduling.

clarifications.q: Two cycles connected by a one-way dependency?
clarifications.a: Two groups. A group needs paths in both directions between every pair.

clarifications.q: Two cycles that share a dataset?
clarifications.a: One group.

clarifications.q: A dataset downstream of a cycle cannot build either. Is it in the group?
clarifications.a: No. Only datasets on a cycle.

clarifications.q: Can I use recursion?
clarifications.a: You can, but pipelines can be long chains; check how deep your search goes.

clarifications.q: What is returned?
clarifications.a: A list of lists of strings, each sorted ascending, groups sorted by first element; [] if there are none.

hints: These are the strongly connected components of the graph. Tarjan's algorithm finds them all in one depth-first pass; Kosaraju's uses two, the second on the reversed graph.
A raw source has no inputs, so it is a component of one on its own and never a group; you can add it to the graph or skip it.
To avoid the recursion limit, keep an explicit stack of (dataset, iterator over its inputs) and update the parent's low-link when a child finishes.
followups: Also report, for each group, the datasets downstream of it that therefore cannot build. How do you get that in linear time?
Propose the fewest declared inputs to remove so that no cycle remains. Why is that hard in general, and what would you do in practice?
Inputs change a few at a time during the day. How would you keep the check fast without recomputing the whole graph each time?
The build should start each dataset as soon as its inputs are ready, across 64 workers. How do the components and the DAG between them drive that scheduler?

rules.ask: What happens on a chain of 100 000 datasets? How would you make the search iterative?
What does a search from every dataset cost on 60 000 datasets, and which single-pass algorithm avoids it?
Kahn's algorithm shows that a cycle exists. How do you get from the datasets it leaves behind to the separate groups?
Union-find merges along edges whatever their direction. Show two datasets it would wrongly put in one group.

templates.title: Supplier record matching: the same postcode and names within one edit
templates.subtopic: blocking, string normalisation, linear within-one-edit check (O(Σ b²·L) with blocking versus O(n²·L) for every pair)

sections.scenario: A distributor integrating supplier lists from several purchasing systems finds the same supplier recorded many times with small differences: case, punctuation, "Ltd" versus "Ltd.", a typo. Before records are linked into one supplier object, a matching step proposes candidate pairs for a reviewer. Comparing every pair of tens of thousands of records is far too slow, and in this exercise only records at the same postcode can be the same supplier.
sections.problem: Implement match_suppliers(records, transpositions=False). Each record is (record_id, name, postcode); postcode may be None. Normalise each name: lower-case it; turn every character other than a–z and 0–9 into a space; split into words; while the last word is one of co, corp, gmbh, inc, limited, llc, ltd, plc, drop it; join the words with single spaces. Normalise each postcode: upper-case it and remove spaces. Two records match when both normalised postcodes are non-empty and equal, both normalised names are non-empty, and the names are within one edit: equal, or one insertion, deletion or substitution of a single character apart (a space is a character). When transpositions is True, swapping two adjacent characters also counts as one edit. Return the matching pairs as (smaller_id, larger_id) tuples, sorted ascending. {{postcode_rule}} {{edit_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 40 000 records, names up to 60 characters, unique integer ids. Comparing every pair will not finish in time; compare only records that can match, and decide "within one edit" in time linear in the name length.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical supplier names, postcodes and ids. Names are ASCII in this exercise. The legal-form list and the one-edit rule are this exercise's matching policy, not a recommendation for any real master-data process.
sections.criteria: Normalises names and postcodes exactly as specified (trailing legal forms only, spaces as characters, empty values never match); blocks by postcode; a linear within-one-edit check including the transposition case; pairs ordered as specified; can explain the cost of large blocks and how deletion keys or better blocking keys address it.

clarifications.q: Are legal-form words removed wherever they appear?
clarifications.a: Only at the end, repeatedly: "Apex Co. Ltd" becomes "apex", but "Co Apex" keeps "co".

clarifications.q: Do "Apex Fasteners" and "ApexFasteners" match?
clarifications.a: Yes. Removing one space is one edit.

clarifications.q: If A matches B and B matches C, do I report A–C?
clarifications.a: Only if A and C match directly. Grouping is a later step.

clarifications.q: A record without a postcode?
clarifications.a: It never matches anything.

clarifications.q: Do I need the exact edit distance?
clarifications.a: No. Only whether it is at most one.

hints: Put records in a dict keyed by normalised postcode and compare pairs only inside each group.

Within one edit: if the lengths differ by more than one, no. Equal lengths: count the positions that differ. Lengths differ by one: walk both until the first difference, then the rest of the shorter must equal the rest of the longer after skipping one character.
A transposition is equal lengths with exactly two differing positions, adjacent, whose characters are swapped.
followups: One industrial estate has 5 000 suppliers at a single postcode. What happens to your running time, and how would keys made by deleting one character from each name find within-one-edit pairs without comparing all pairs in the block?
Postcodes themselves have typos. How would you block so those pairs are not lost, and what does it cost?
The pairs go to a reviewer before records merge into one supplier object. How do you turn pairs into proposed groups, and what stops one bad pair from chaining two different suppliers together?
How would you measure the precision and recall of this matcher without labelling every pair?

rules.ask: A full edit-distance table costs O(L²) per pair. You only need to know whether the distance is at most one. How do you decide that in O(L)?
Sorting by postcode and scanning runs of equal postcodes is blocking too. How does it compare with a dict of lists?
The rule here is exact: within one edit. What would a similarity threshold change for reviewers, and how would you choose it?
The task asks for direct pairs. If you grouped them transitively, what could chaining do to two different suppliers?

templates.title: Sensor outliers against a rolling median per machine
templates.subtopic: sliding-window median with lazy deletion, per-key windows

sections.scenario: A manufacturer streams readings from sensors on its presses, pumps and kilns into an integrated data platform, where each machine is an object that maintenance planners watch. A reading that is far from the machine's recent normal behaviour should raise a flag on the machine. Averages are pulled about by the very spikes the planners want to find, so the plant's rule uses the median: a reading is an outlier when it is more than d units from the median of the same machine's previous w readings. The check runs on every reading, for every machine, as the data arrives.
sections.problem: Implement sensor_outliers(readings, w, d, exclude_outliers=False). readings is a list of (machine_id, value) in time order, with the machines interleaved, and values are integers. For each reading, look at the previous w readings of the same machine (its window). If the machine does not yet have w earlier readings, the reading is not checked. Otherwise it is an outlier when |value − median(window)| > d. Return the positions in readings (0-based, ascending) of every outlier. {{window_rule}} {{exclude_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 300 000 readings and up to 100 000 readings in a window, which is about a day at one reading a second. w ≥ 1, d ≥ 0, and values are integers below 10⁶ in absolute value. Something close to O(n log w) is expected. Work that grows with w on every reading is too slow when the window is a day long.
sections.assumptions: Machines, units, rates and thresholds are hypothetical. Readings arrive in time order with no ties to break. Machines are independent: one machine's readings never enter another machine's window.
sections.criteria: Per-machine windows of exactly the previous w readings; warm-up readings never checked; a strict > d boundary; exact comparison for even windows; dropouts skipped and never counted; flagged readings kept out of the window when asked; a structure that gives the median in O(log w) per reading (two heaps with lazy deletion, or an equivalent); a clear complexity argument against sorting or a sorted list; sensible answers on spread, ordering and streaming state.

clarifications.q: Is "more than d" strict?
clarifications.a: Yes. A reading exactly d from the median is not an outlier.

clarifications.q: Are the first readings of a machine checked against a shorter window?
clarifications.a: No. A reading is checked only when the machine already has w earlier readings in its window. The warm-up readings are never flagged.

clarifications.q: Does the window include the reading being checked?
clarifications.a: No. It is the previous w readings of that machine, before this one.

clarifications.q: What if the median is not a whole number?
clarifications.a: It can be only when w is even. Compare exactly. Doubling both sides keeps everything in integers.

clarifications.q: Can I return a list of machine ids?
clarifications.a: No. Return positions in readings, so the platform can mark those exact readings.

hints: Keep one window per machine. The question is how to get the median of a window that loses its oldest reading and gains a new one each step.

Two heaps (a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half) give the median from their tops. Removing an arbitrary reading from a heap is the hard part: you do not have to remove it at once, only before it reaches a top.

Give each reading in a machine's window a sequence number. A heap entry whose number is older than the window's start is stale, and you discard it when it reaches the top. Track how many live entries each heap holds so you can rebalance.
followups: Planners want the flag to say how unusual the reading is, not just yes or no. How would you add a robust spread, such as the median absolute deviation, and what does it cost to keep it up to date?
Readings for one machine arrive out of order by a few seconds after a network blip. What does your window mean then, and what would you change?
The plant has 40 000 sensors. How would you run this as a stream, how is state partitioned and checkpointed, and what happens to a machine's window on a restart?
Twelve machines start flagging at the same minute. How would you tell a real process change from a sensor or gateway fault before anyone is paged?

rules.ask: Inserting into and deleting from a Python list moves the entries after that position. With a window of 86 400 readings, how many entries move per reading, and how long does a day of readings take?
What does sorting the window cost per reading at w = 86 400, and for 240 000 readings?
The reading leaving the window is somewhere inside one of your heaps. How do you remove it, and how do you know which heap it is in?
The median of an even window can end in .5. Show that your comparison is exact at the boundary, or rewrite it in integers.
That is a fine structure if you can use it. Without a library, what would you build, and what does each operation cost?

templates.title: Downtime rolled up an asset hierarchy
templates.subtopic: bottom-up aggregation in one pass, iterative traversal

sections.scenario: A manufacturer models its plants as linked objects: a site has production lines, a line has machines, a machine has components, and some components hold sub-assemblies. Downtime is recorded against whichever asset failed, from a whole line stopped for a power dip to a single worn bearing. Operations leaders ask the same question at every level of the hierarchy: how much downtime is there in this site, this line, this machine, counting everything below it? A dashboard sends thousands of such questions at once, most of them for sites, lines and machines.
sections.problem: Implement rollup_downtime(assets, events, queries, drill=False). assets is a list of (asset_id, parent_id), with parent_id None for a site, listed in any order. events is a list of (asset_id, minutes, kind) downtime records. queries is a list of asset ids. For each query, return the total minutes of downtime recorded on that asset and on every asset below it, in query order. An asset id that is not in assets returns -1. {{event_rule}} {{drill_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 assets, 300 000 records and 200 000 queries. Every parent named in assets is itself listed, there are no cycles, and the hierarchy is a few levels deep. Minutes are positive integers. Something close to O(n + e + q) is expected. Walking each queried asset's subtree is too slow when most queries name a site or a line.
sections.assumptions: Plants, assets and minutes are hypothetical. Downtime records do not overlap in any way that matters here: the rollup is a plain sum, not a union of time intervals.
sections.criteria: Correct subtree totals including an asset's own records; assets accepted in any order; -1 for unknown assets and 0 for assets without downtime; planned work and retired assets excluded; the drill-down tie rule and None when no child has downtime; one bottom-up pass in O(n + e + q) with an iterative order; a clear argument against per-query walks; credible answers on incremental updates, moves over time and interval overlap.

clarifications.q: Does a site's own record count for the site?
clarifications.a: Yes. A record on an asset counts for that asset and for every asset above it.

clarifications.q: Are assets listed parents first?
clarifications.a: No. A component can appear before its machine and its site.

clarifications.q: What do I return for an asset with no downtime?
clarifications.a: 0. Only an asset that is not in assets returns -1.

clarifications.q: Can the same asset be queried twice?
clarifications.a: Yes, and each query gets its own answer in the output.

clarifications.q: Can I use recursion?
clarifications.a: Yes for this depth, but say what happens if a source system ever sends a hierarchy thousands of levels deep.

hints: Every query asks about a subtree. If you knew every asset's subtree total, each query would be one dictionary lookup.
A child's total is finished before its parent's. Find an order in which every asset comes after all of its descendants, then add each asset's total into its parent's.
A pre-order from the sites with an explicit stack, read backwards, is such an order. No recursion is needed.
followups: Records arrive all day. How would you keep the totals current without recomputing the whole plant for each new record?
A machine is moved from one line to another at noon. Which totals change, and how would you answer "downtime by line for yesterday" both before and after the move?
Leaders want hours of downtime, not the sum of records: two overlapping records on one machine are one stoppage. What changes, and what does it cost?
The same question is asked of a hierarchy with 50 million assets across many customers' plants. Where would you compute the rollup, and how would you serve the queries?

rules.ask: What is Python's default recursion limit, and what happens if one sub-assembly chain is 5 000 levels deep?
Adding each record to every ancestor costs records × depth. When is that fine, and when would you switch to one bottom-up pass?
A query for a site visits every asset below it. With 30 000 site queries, how many visits is that?
Your cache helps repeated queries. What does the first query for each line still cost, and what does the whole run cost in the worst case?
Why should a drill-down choose the same child every time when two children are tied, and who would notice if it did not?

templates.title: Debug the ontology object sync
templates.subtopic: object sync from a backing dataset, keys, deletes, casts, time zones, nulls

sections.scenario: In this exercise's model, an operational application shows objects (work orders, shipments, hospital beds) that are kept in sync with a backing dataset from a source system. A sync step applies the source's change rows to the object store: upserts and deletes, with every property value arriving as text and cast to the type the object type declares. Users have reported several problems. Some objects appear twice after the source system renumbered them. An object that was deleted and re-created in the source has vanished. Every "hazardous" flag reads true. Due times are hours off for one site. A carrier that was removed in the source still shows on the object. The sync function below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix sync_objects(store, changes, schema, source_offset) so that it meets this specification. store maps primary key to the object's properties, already typed. changes is a list of change rows in commit order. You may update store in place, and you return it. {{replay_rule}}

  1. delete {"op", "pk"} removes the object with that key. A delete for a key that is not in the store changes nothing.
  2. upsert {"op", "pk", "props"} creates the object if it does not exist, or updates it. Rows are applied strictly in commit order, so an upsert after a delete of the same key creates a new object from that row alone.
  3. Changed primary keys. An upsert may carry "old_pk": the source changed the row's key from old_pk to pk. If old_pk is in the store, the object moves: it is removed from old_pk and stored under pk with its properties, and then the row's props are applied. If old_pk is not in the store, the row is a plain upsert of pk. The new key is never already in the store.
  4. Null versus missing. A property missing from props keeps its current value. A property present with the value None is set to None. A property not named in schema is ignored.
  5. Casts. Raw values are text. "int": an integer, possibly with leading zeros or a sign. "bool": "true" or "false" in any letter case. "str": as is. "timestamp": YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS (or with T between date and time), optionally followed by Z or an offset ±HH:MM. Convert to UTC and store as YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ. A timestamp with no zone is in the source system's local time, which is source_offset minutes east of UTC.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 change rows, processed in linear time.
sections.assumptions: Object types, keys and values are hypothetical and simplified. Change rows are delivered once and in commit order. Source offsets are fixed for the exercise: daylight-saving changes are out of scope.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its user-visible symptom; rows applied in commit order; a changed key moves the object; "false" casts to False in any case; zone-less timestamps use the source offset, zoned ones their own; explicit null clears and missing keeps; properties outside the schema ignored; minimal, linear fixes with a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Should deletes be applied after upserts to save work?
clarifications.a: No. Rows are applied in commit order. The order is what makes a delete followed by a re-insert mean what it says.

clarifications.q: If a property is missing from an upsert, should it be cleared?
clarifications.a: No. Missing means unchanged. Only an explicit None clears it.

clarifications.q: What is source_offset for a timestamp that has its own offset?
clarifications.a: Unused. Its own Z or ±HH:MM decides. source_offset applies only to timestamps with no zone.

clarifications.q: After a key change, do I keep anything under the old key?
clarifications.a: No. The object now lives only under the new key.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Run a renumbered object through the code: which keys exist in the store afterwards?
Write down a delete and a re-create of the same key, in that order. What does the code do with them, and in which order?
In Python, what is bool("false")?
Read the timestamp branch for an input with no zone: which offset does it use?
What does the loop over props do with a value of None?
followups: The source system sends a full snapshot each night instead of change rows. How do you find deletes and key changes from two snapshots, and what can you no longer tell apart?
Users also edit some of these properties in the application. How do you merge their edits with the source's updates, and who wins?
The source switches one site to daylight saving time. Which stored timestamps are now wrong, and how would you have prevented it?
A cast fails on one row of 200 000 (the text "n/a" for an integer). What should the sync do with that row and with the rest of the batch?

rules.ask: With full snapshots, a renumbered row looks like a delete and an insert. What do you lose on the object, such as links and user edits, and how would you detect the renumbering instead?
How does your merge tell a property set to None from one that was not sent at all?
What does your parser return for a timestamp with no zone, and where does the source's offset come from?
Show a sequence of rows where applying all upserts before all deletes gives a different object store.
Which other text values would you expect from a source system for a boolean, and what should happen to one you do not recognise?

templates.title: Writeback from operational apps to source systems
templates.subtopic: writeback, optimistic concurrency, retries, audit trail

sections.scenario: A distributor's planners work in operational applications built on an integrated data platform. In this exercise's model, they act on objects (they reassign a work order, change a purchase order's quantity, put a shipment on hold) about {{actions_per_day}} times a day. Each action must be written back to the system of record it came from, and there are {{systems}} of them: an ERP, a warehouse system, a maintenance system and others, each with its own API and limits. Data flows the other way too: each source is synced back into the platform, and the slowest sync lags by {{sync_delay}}. Meanwhile, people keep editing the same records directly in the source systems.
sections.problem: Design how an action taken in the application reaches the source system and how the platform knows what happened to it. Cover the action record and what it captures, how an action becomes a write to a source system, how you detect that the source record changed since the user saw it, what the user sees while a write is pending, applied, rejected or in conflict, retries and failures (including a source system that is down for {{outage}}), the order of several actions on the same record, how the next sync from the source confirms or contradicts the action, and the audit trail.
sections.constraints: A retried write must never apply an action twice in the source. An action must never silently overwrite a newer change made in the source. Every action, its outcome and the user who took it must be answerable a year later. One slow or failing source system must not hold up actions bound for the others. The application must not show a value as current that the source has rejected.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, systems and delays are hypothetical. Each source system offers a write API that returns the record's new version or an error, and most of them can read a record's current version. You may use common building blocks: a transactional database, a durable queue or log, workers and a scheduler.
sections.criteria: A durable action log written before any external call, with the user, purpose, inputs and the version seen; conditional writes or an equivalent conflict check per source capability; explicit action states visible to the user; retries that are safe because each write carries a stable action identity the source can recognise or that can be verified before retrying; per-system queues and limits for isolation; ordering per record; compensation for multi-record actions; confirmation by matching the next sync; an audit trail that can answer who, what, when and outcome; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Does the action change the object in the platform immediately?
clarifications.a: Your choice, and you must explain it. Users want to see their change. The source remains the system of record.

clarifications.q: Do all source systems support versions or ETags?
clarifications.a: Most do. Plan for one that has only a last-modified timestamp, and one that has nothing.

clarifications.q: What should happen on a conflict?
clarifications.a: Never overwrite silently. Who resolves it, and how, is part of your design.

clarifications.q: Are actions on different records independent?
clarifications.a: Mostly. Some actions change two records, such as moving stock between two locations, and both must happen or neither.

clarifications.q: Who reads the audit trail?
clarifications.a: Operations leads investigating a bad decision, and auditors checking who changed what.

hints: Record the action first, durably, with the version of the record the user saw. Everything else (the write, the retries, the confirmation) is processing of that record.
A conditional write ("apply only if the record is still at version v") turns a lost update into a detectable conflict.
The next sync from the source is your ground truth. Plan how a pending action is matched to the change it caused.
followups: A source system is down for {{outage}}. Walk through what the user sees, what queues up, and what happens when it comes back.
Two planners act on the same purchase order within a minute, one in the application and one directly in the ERP. Walk through both orders of arrival.
An action that moves stock changes two records in the warehouse system, and the second write fails. What do you do?
With {{sync_delay}} of sync lag, a user sees their action applied, and an hour later the synced data shows the old value. What happened, and what does the user see?
At {{actions_per_day}} actions a day, the audit trail has to answer "every change to this record and why" in seconds. How do you store it?

rules.ask: The write timed out, so you do not know whether it was applied. What does your retry send, and how does the source system know it is the same action?
The source changed the quantity after the user loaded the page. Under last write wins, whose change survives, and who finds out?
One source system has no versions at all. How do you detect a conflict there, and what does it cost?
The source systems do not share transactions. How do you undo the first write when the second fails, and what does the user see meanwhile?
How does the action log relate to the object the user sees, and what does a user see after a rejected action?

incidents: The ERP is down for {{outage}} during the morning planning window, and planners keep acting on objects bound for it.
A deploy of one connector retries timed-out writes without checking whether they were applied, and some purchase-order quantity changes are applied twice.
The slowest source's sync, {{sync_delay}} behind, overwrites the platform's view of 3% of records that users changed that afternoon.

templates.title: Branching a data pipeline and merging it back
templates.subtopic: branches, incremental rebuilds of affected datasets, output comparison, merge

sections.scenario: A utility's data team maintains a pipeline graph of about {{datasets}} datasets: meter readings, outages, customer accounts, asset records and the reports built on them. Engineers want to change a transform the way they change code: on a branch, with their own outputs, compared with production before anyone relies on them, and then merged. About {{branches}} branches are open at any time. Rebuilding the whole graph takes {{rebuild_cost}}, and the largest dataset holds {{largest}}, so a branch cannot copy everything.
sections.problem: Design branching for the pipeline. Cover what a branch is (code, data or both), how a branch reads datasets it has not changed, how you find and rebuild only the datasets affected by a change, how branch outputs are stored without copying unchanged data, how a branch's outputs are compared with main's (schema, row counts, keys, values), what happens when main moves on while a branch is open, what merging does to code and data, and how access controls carry over to branch outputs.
sections.constraints: A branch must never change what main's users see. Unchanged datasets must not be copied. A branch's comparison must be against the same inputs main used, or say clearly that it is not. A merge must leave main in a state that a fresh build from main's code would also produce. Every branch output must carry the same access restrictions as the data it was derived from.
sections.assumptions: Sizes, counts and costs are hypothetical. Every transform declares its inputs and outputs, and datasets are stored as versioned files in object storage. Transforms are deterministic given the same inputs, except where noted. This is this exercise's model, not any product's.
sections.criteria: A branch defined over code and dataset versions with fall-back to main for unchanged datasets; affected-set computation from the dependency graph; copy-free storage of unchanged data; comparisons by key with schema, row and value differences against recorded inputs; a clear policy for main moving on and for concurrent merges; a merge that leaves main reproducible; inherited access restrictions on every branch output; compute isolation and garbage collection; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Does a branch see main's latest data or a frozen copy?
clarifications.a: Your choice, and you must explain it. Both have costs.

clarifications.q: Can a branch change a dataset's schema?
clarifications.a: Yes, and the comparison must show it.

clarifications.q: What does "affected" mean?
clarifications.a: A dataset whose transform changed on the branch, and everything downstream of one.

clarifications.q: What happens to branch data after a merge?
clarifications.a: Your choice. Say whether main reuses it or rebuilds.

clarifications.q: Are some transforms non-deterministic?
clarifications.a: A few use the current time or sample rows. Plan for them in the comparison.

hints: A branch can be a pointer: for each dataset, either the branch's own version or a fall-back to main's version at a recorded point.
The datasets to rebuild are the changed transforms' outputs and their descendants in the graph. Nothing upstream needs to run.
Compare on keys, not just counts: rows only in main, rows only in the branch, and rows whose values changed, per column.
followups: Main has rebuilt a source dataset twice since the branch was opened. What does the branch's comparison mean now, and how would you make it fair?
Two branches change the same transform in different ways and both want to merge. What happens?
A changed transform near the top of the graph affects 70% of the datasets. What does a branch build cost, and how would you make it affordable?
With {{branches}} branches open, storage keeps growing. What do you keep, for how long, and what do you garbage-collect?
A branch output derived from a restricted dataset is shared in a review. How do you ensure the restriction travelled with it?

rules.ask: Copying {{largest}} per branch with {{branches}} branches open costs how much storage, and what do you do instead?
A full rebuild takes {{rebuild_cost}}. Which datasets actually need to run for a one-line change in one transform?
Counts can match while every value in a column is wrong. What comparison would catch that?
For data, not code, what does a conflict look like, and when must main rebuild after the merge?
A pinned snapshot makes the comparison fair. How old can it get before the comparison stops being useful?

incidents: A branch build of a changed transform near the top of the graph starts rebuilding datasets whose total rebuild time is most of {{rebuild_cost}}, and it competes with main's nightly build for compute.
A merged branch passes its comparison, but main's next build produces different numbers because the branch had compared against main as it was two weeks earlier.
A branch output derived from a restricted customer-account dataset is readable by everyone on the branch's project because the branch's dataset was created without the inherited restriction.

templates.title: The ontology as data — object types, properties, links, actions and an object as it stood on a date
templates.subtopic: metadata as versioned data, stable property ids, bitemporal object history, action log

sections.scenario: A manufacturer models its operations as an ontology: about {{object_types}} object types (asset, work order, part, supplier, plant and so on), each with typed properties; link types between object types (a work order is for an asset, a part is supplied by a supplier); and action types, the named edits a user can make in an operational application ("reassign work order", "flag part as defective"), each changing one or more objects at once. About {{objects}} objects are backed by pipeline datasets and also edited by users; together they make about {{edits_per_day}} property changes a day. The ontology itself keeps changing, about {{schema_changes_per_week}} definition changes a week: properties are added, renamed, retyped or deprecated, and link types change cardinality. Auditors and analysts ask the same kind of question again and again: "what did this work order look like on 3 March, which action changed it, and what did the schema say then?"
sections.problem: Design the data model that stores the ontology's definitions and the objects' history as data. Cover: the definition tables (object types, properties with stable ids and display names, link types with cardinality, action types with their parameters and the edits they make) and how a definition change is recorded as a new version; how object property values are stored (wide per type, long per property, or events with snapshots) and with which time columns; how an action's submission, validation, and the edits it applied are logged so that edits made together stay together; and how to reconstruct one object as of a date, both under the schema in force then and under today's schema.
sections.constraints: A property keeps one stable id for life; a rename changes only its display name. History is append-only: a correction is a new record, never an update in place. Reconstructing one object as of a date takes seconds. A change of a property's type never silently rewrites stored history. An object type is deprecated, never dropped, while any object or history row refers to it.
sections.assumptions: Volumes and rates are hypothetical. The model is this exercise's, not a description of any product's internals. Objects have a stable primary key from their backing data. Times are UTC. Users edit only through actions; pipelines write through their own sync.
sections.criteria: Definitions modelled as versioned data with stable ids separate from display names; instances keyed by those ids; a clear time model (valid and recorded time, or an equivalent with an explicit argument); an action log that groups edits and records rejections; a reconstruction path for one object at a date under both schemas; a growth estimate with snapshots and compaction; type changes and renames handled without rewriting history; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is "as of 3 March" about when a value was true or when we knew it?
clarifications.a: Both are asked. A pipeline correction loaded on 10 March can fix a value that was wrong since 1 March; auditors need "as we knew it on 5 March" and analysts "as we know it now".

clarifications.q: What happens when a property changes type, say text to date?
clarifications.a: Treat it as a new version of the property's definition with a stated conversion. Old values stay as they were stored; how they are read under the new type is your design.

clarifications.q: Can an action fail?
clarifications.a: Yes. Submissions are validated; a rejected one changes nothing but is logged with the reason.

clarifications.q: Do pipeline syncs and user edits ever touch the same property?
clarifications.a: Yes, and that conflict is the subject of another question. Here, record which writer produced each value.

clarifications.q: Can a link carry properties of its own?
clarifications.a: Many-to-many links can, for example the quantity of a part on a work order. Decide how they are stored.

hints: Separate definitions (types, properties, link types, action types) from instances (objects, values, links, action runs), and version the definitions with valid_from and valid_to.
Key every value by the property's stable id, never by its display name.
Two time axes answer the two questions: when a value was true (valid time) and when the platform recorded it (recorded time).
followups: A property status is renamed lifecycle_state and two of its allowed values are merged. Show what a query over last quarter returns, before and after the change.
A correction loaded today fixes a value that was wrong since last month. Show the rows, and the predicates for "as we knew it on the 5th" and "as we know it now".
One action edited three objects and one of the edits failed validation. How does your log show what happened, and what did the other two objects end up with?
At {{objects}} objects and {{edits_per_day}} changes a day, estimate the history's growth. What do you snapshot, how often, and how do you compact old history without losing what auditors need?

rules.ask: A property changes from text to date across millions of objects. How does a reader of your JSON tell an old string from a new date, and how is a query over last year written?
A dashboard reads 30 properties of 2 million objects. How many rows is that in your layout, and what do you materialise to keep it fast?
Definitions change {{schema_changes_per_week}} times a week. What does each change cost your wide tables, and how do you keep last year's shape for history?
Write the two timestamps for a correction loaded today about last month, and the exact predicate for "as we knew it on the 10th".
An auditor asks for the object at 14:32 on a given day. What does your daily snapshot answer, and what fills the gap between snapshots?

incidents: A property rename was deployed as a new property plus the deletion of the old one. Every report spanning the change shows the property empty before the rename date, and history for objects of that type no longer joins across it.

A pipeline backfill re-loaded six months of corrected values and stamped each row's recorded time with its valid time. "As we knew it" views for last quarter now show values nobody saw then, and an audit of decisions made in that quarter reads the wrong data.

With {{schema_changes_per_week}} definition changes a week, a link type's cardinality changed from one-to-many to many-to-many. Older links have no row in the new link table, and an application shows them as missing.

templates.title: Markings and purpose-based access as data — inheritance along lineage, expiring grants, and who could read what when
templates.subtopic: access metadata over lineage, effective markings, time-bounded purpose grants, access audit

sections.scenario: A pharmaceutical manufacturer integrates its manufacturing, quality and commercial data into about {{datasets}} datasets used by {{users}} people. In this exercise's model, a dataset carries markings (there are {{markings}} kinds, for example trial participant data, supplier pricing, unreleased financials). A user can read a dataset only if they hold every marking on it and have an active purpose grant for it: a request stating the purpose ("batch deviation investigation", "quarterly supplier review"), approved by the data owner, that expires after {{grant_days}} days unless renewed. A dataset derived from others inherits the union of its inputs' markings, unless an approved release step removes a marking (for example, an aggregation that leaves no participant-level rows). Compliance asks two kinds of question: "who could read this dataset on 4 June, and why?", and "which datasets carried trial participant data on 4 June, and through which inputs?"
sections.problem: Design the data model for markings, lineage, purpose grants and the access audit. Cover: markings applied directly to datasets and their history; the lineage graph between dataset versions; how effective (inherited) markings are computed and stored, and how they change when an upstream marking or an edge in the lineage changes; release steps that remove a marking, with their approvals; users' marking eligibility; purpose grants with requests, approvals, renewals, expiry and revocation; read events; and the queries that answer "could user U read dataset D at time t, and through which grant and markings?", for any past t.
sections.constraints: Every answer about the past is reproducible: what was effective at time t is never recomputed from today's state. A dataset's effective markings never lose an inherited marking except through an approved release step. Grants expire exactly at their stated expiry. Read events are append-only. The model describes the rules; how a platform enforces them at read time is out of scope.
sections.assumptions: Counts and durations are hypothetical; the access rules are this exercise's model, not any product's. Lineage is known for every derived dataset from the pipeline that builds it. Users' marking eligibility is managed elsewhere and arrives as dated changes.
sections.criteria: Direct markings, lineage, effective markings and grants modelled as time-bounded data; inheritance at dataset-version grain with a stated propagation rule and lag; release steps as approved, scoped records tied to a specific output version; grants with purpose, approval, renewal, expiry and non-retroactive revocation; an append-only read log that records the grant used; a reproducible "could U read D at t" query; incremental recomputation at scale; each incident contained, corrected and guarded, without describing any product's enforcement internals.

clarifications.q: If one input of a derived dataset is marked, is the whole output marked?
clarifications.a: Yes. Inheritance is the union of all inputs' effective markings, at the dataset version that was built.

clarifications.q: Can a marking be removed upstream?
clarifications.a: Yes, by the owner, with a reason. What happens downstream is part of your design; say whether it is immediate or waits for a rebuild.

clarifications.q: Does a renewal create a new grant?
clarifications.a: Your choice; the audit must show the original request, every renewal and who approved each.

clarifications.q: What exactly is a read?
clarifications.a: A logged event: user, dataset version, time, the grant used, and the application or query that read it.

clarifications.q: Is revoking a grant retroactive?
clarifications.a: No. It stops future reads; reads made before revocation stay valid in the audit.

hints: Store direct markings and lineage edges with validity; compute effective markings as a derived, versioned table keyed by dataset version.
A grant is an interval with a purpose, an approver and a reason; renewals extend it with their own records.
"Could U read D at t" is a join of three time-bounded facts: U's eligible markings at t, D's effective markings at t, and U's grants for D active at t.
followups: Lineage forms a diamond: dataset C reads A and B, both of which read a marked dataset R. R's marking is removed. When does C lose it, and what does the audit show for the hours in between?
Write, in words or SQL, the check for reads that happened outside an active grant or without every required marking.
A grant of {{grant_days}} days expires mid-investigation and the user renews a day late. What does the model record for the gap, and which reads in it are flagged?
At {{datasets}} datasets, a marking added to one raw dataset reaches thousands of descendants. How do you recompute effective markings incrementally, and how long may they lag?

An approved release step removed trial participant data from an aggregate, and the aggregate's code later changed so that small groups re-appear. How does your model notice that the approval no longer covers the output?

rules.ask: Two analysts in the same group have the same markings but different purposes. Where does purpose live in your design, and how does the audit show which purpose a read served?
A marking is added upstream while a downstream build is running. Which version of the output carries it, and what about reads of the previous version?
Your effective markings are materialised. An upstream edge is added. What exactly is invalidated, and what is the read path during recomputation?
A grant is revoked at 10:00. A long-running query started at 09:58 reads until 10:05. What does your audit record?
Is a grant valid at exactly its expiry time? Write the comparison and say why.

incidents: A marking was added to a raw dataset of supplier pricing; the job that recomputes effective markings lagged for hours, and a derived dashboard stayed readable by users without that marking. Compliance asks exactly who read it in that window.

A batch of grants created on the same day for a {{grant_days}}-day project expired together on a holiday. Hundreds of analysts lost access mid-investigation, and the renewals approved in bulk the next morning carried no stated purpose.
A release step approved for an aggregate was reused when the aggregate's inputs changed; the output now includes participant-level rows while carrying no trial participant data marking.

templates.title: Decision workflows as data — alerts, cases, assignments, closing actions and outcomes weeks later
templates.subtopic: case lifecycle, assignment history, actions with parameters, delayed outcome labels

sections.scenario: A food distributor runs its operations from applications built on integrated data. About {{rules}} rules raise {{alerts_per_day}} alerts a day on objects: a refrigerated shipment whose temperature drifts, a purchase order a supplier is late to confirm, a store forecast to run out of a staple. Related alerts are grouped into a case, and cases are routed to {{inboxes}} team inboxes, where planners pick them up, reassign them, and act: reroute a shipment, expedite an order, accept a delay, or dismiss the case as a false alarm. Each action is recorded with its parameters. Whether a decision was good is known only later: about {{outcome_weeks}} weeks afterwards the distributor knows whether the shipment was accepted in specification, whether the store ran out, and what the expedite cost. Leaders want time to first action, false-alarm rate per rule, workload per inbox, and which actions tend to lead to better outcomes.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: alerts (rule, rule version, the object and the values that triggered it), cases and the alert-to-case grouping (which can change), the case lifecycle and its states, assignments and reassignments to inboxes and people, actions with parameters and their effect on objects, the closing resolution, and outcomes that arrive weeks later and can be revised. Define precisely: time to first action, false-alarm rate per rule (and its cohort), and an outcome comparison by action type that does not mistake selection for effect. Say which facts and grains answer these questions, and what is reported per inbox versus per person.
sections.constraints: Case history is append-only; the current state is derived. Every action records who took it, when, with which parameters, and on which object version. Outcomes are labelled with their source and the date they became known. Workload and timing are reported per inbox and per rule, not used to rank individual planners.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, rule counts and delays are hypothetical. Rules are versioned. A case can contain alerts on several objects (for example several shipments on one truck). Outcomes come from other systems (receiving, store sales, invoices) through pipelines.
sections.criteria: Alerts, cases, membership, assignments, actions, resolutions and outcomes modelled as separate, time-stamped facts; rule versions and triggering values on alerts; derived current state; precise definitions of time to first action and false-alarm rate with cohorts; outcomes with known_at and revisions, and a stated close for monthly reports; caution about selection effects; reporting per inbox and rule rather than ranking people; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can an alert move to another case?
clarifications.a: Yes, when a planner merges or splits cases. The history must show it.

clarifications.q: When does time to first action start?
clarifications.a: Your choice: when the first alert fired, or when the case reached an inbox. Define it, and say what happens on reassignment.

clarifications.q: Can a closed case reopen?
clarifications.a: Yes, if a new alert joins it within a window you choose.

clarifications.q: Are dismissals always false alarms?
clarifications.a: No. A planner may dismiss because someone already fixed it outside the application. Your resolution codes should let you tell these apart.

clarifications.q: Can an outcome change after it is recorded?
clarifications.a: Yes; a credit note can arrive after the first invoice, for example.

hints: Separate events (alert raised, case created, assigned, action taken, closed, reopened) from current-state tables, and derive the latter.
Store rule version and the triggering values on each alert; a rule change otherwise looks like a change in the world.
Outcomes are their own table keyed by case (or object) with a known_at date, so "what did we know then" stays answerable.
followups: A rule's threshold was changed mid-month. Show how your model reports the false-alarm rate before and after, and why the two are not directly comparable.
Expedited shipments had better outcomes than accepted delays. What else could explain that, and what would your data need to say more?
A case was merged into another after two days. How do timing metrics treat each of the original alerts?

At {{alerts_per_day}} alerts a day and outcomes arriving {{outcome_weeks}} weeks later, which facts do you keep at event grain, which as accumulating snapshots per case, and when is a month's outcome report final?

rules.ask: A case went open → assigned → reassigned → closed → reopened. With a status column, how do you compute time to first action for last month?
Which dismissals count as false alarms, and how does your resolution code tell "not a problem" from "already fixed elsewhere"?
Planners take harder cases in different inboxes. What would a per-person comparison actually measure, and what would you report instead?
The outcome for a case is revised five weeks later. Which reports change, and how does a reader know which version they saw?
Planners chose which cases to expedite. What would let you estimate the effect of expediting rather than the difference between the cases chosen?

incidents: A rule change doubled one rule's alerts overnight. Inboxes filled, time to first action rose for every rule, and the dashboard attributed the slowdown to planners rather than to the rule version.
A cleanup job closed thousands of stale cases with the resolution "dismissed". The false-alarm rate per rule jumped for the month, and two useful rules were proposed for retirement.
Outcomes arrive about {{outcome_weeks}} weeks after a case closes; a weekly report treated cases with no outcome yet as failures, so the newest actions always looked worst.

templates.title: Scenarios as data — what-if copies of objects, proposed changes, approvals and plan against actual
templates.subtopic: copy-on-write overlays on objects, scenario lineage, approval and apply, plan-versus-actual

sections.scenario: A manufacturer's planners decide how to respond to disruptions by building what-if scenarios over the integrated picture of plants, lines, parts, suppliers and orders (about {{objects_in_scope}} objects in scope). A scenario starts from the live objects at some moment and proposes changes: move a part's production from one plant to another for {{horizon_weeks}} weeks, add a second supplier, delay a batch of orders. Each scenario holds up to about {{edits_per_scenario}} proposed edits, can be copied and varied into a new scenario, and is scored by models (capacity, cost, late orders). About {{open_scenarios}} scenarios are open at once. A chosen scenario is approved and applied: its edits become real changes made through actions. Months later, leaders want to compare what the chosen scenario predicted with what actually happened.
sections.problem: Design the data model for scenarios. Cover: the scenario entity and its lineage (copied from which scenario, based on the live data as of when); how proposed edits are stored without copying the base objects; how a reader resolves an object's value inside a scenario; what happens when the live data changes under an open scenario (pinned to its base time, or rebased) and how conflicts are detected; model runs and their outputs per scenario, with the model version and inputs; approval and application (which edits were applied, by which actions, and what failed); and the plan-versus-actual comparison over the {{horizon_weeks}}-week horizon.
sections.constraints: A scenario never changes live data until it is applied. Reading an object inside a scenario returns the base value unless the scenario (or its ancestors) proposed a change. A scored result is reproducible: same scenario version, model version and inputs give the same numbers. An approved scenario version is frozen. Applying is auditable edit by edit.
sections.assumptions: Counts and horizons are hypothetical. The model is this exercise's, not a description of any product's internals. Live object history is kept with valid and recorded time (assume it exists). Models are versioned and deterministic given their inputs.
sections.criteria: Scenarios as a base time plus overlays with lineage, never full copies; an explicit read path through ancestors and base; pinned versus rebased semantics with conflict detection by base version; frozen approved versions; model runs recorded with model version and inputs; apply as audited edit-by-edit outcomes; a plan-versus-actual model that separates base drift, model error and execution gaps; storage and read-path estimates; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: When a scenario is copied, are its edits copied too?
clarifications.a: Your choice: copy them or inherit them from the parent. The read path and storage differ; say which and why.

clarifications.q: The live data changed after a scenario was created. Which values does the scenario see?
clarifications.a: Decide between pinned (the base as of creation) and rebased (the latest base plus the scenario's edits). Planners need both, explicitly.

clarifications.q: Can an edit fail when applied?
clarifications.a: Yes, if the object it changes has moved on or been deleted. The application must record it.

clarifications.q: What is "actual" in plan-versus-actual?
clarifications.a: The live objects and outcomes over the horizon, as recorded after the fact; say which version of them the comparison reads.

hints: Store a scenario as a base reference (a time) plus an overlay of edits keyed by (object, property); copy-on-write, never a copy of the objects.
Resolve a value by checking the scenario's overlay, then its ancestors', then the base as of the base time.
Record base version per edit, so applying can detect that the live value changed since the edit was proposed.
followups: Scenario B was copied from A, then A was edited again. Does B see A's new edit? Show your read path for one property.
Estimate storage for {{open_scenarios}} open scenarios with {{edits_per_scenario}} edits each, versus copying the objects in scope. Which reads become slower with overlays, and how do you index them?

The chosen scenario predicted 40 late orders and 112 occurred. Which tables do you join to explain the gap, separating "the world changed" from "the model was wrong" from "we did not apply what we approved"?
A planner rebases an old scenario onto today's data, and 300 of its edits now conflict. What does your model record, and what does the planner see?

rules.ask: With {{open_scenarios}} open scenarios over {{objects_in_scope}} objects, how much storage is that, and what happens to a copy when the base changes?
A scenario four levels deep reads one property. Walk through the lookups, and say how you keep that fast.
A rebased scenario's score changed overnight without anyone editing it. How does a planner see why?
The cost model was upgraded after approval. Which numbers does plan-versus-actual use, and where is that recorded?
Half the approved edits applied and half failed because objects had moved on. Is the scenario applied? What do the plan-versus-actual numbers compare against?

incidents: An early version stored each scenario as a full copy of the objects in scope. With {{open_scenarios}} scenarios open over {{objects_in_scope}} objects, storage grew past budget in a month and scenario creation took tens of minutes.

A scenario approved against a three-week-old base was applied; a supplier it relied on had since been marked inactive, and dozens of its edits were applied on top of changes made after the base without anyone being shown a conflict.
A plan-versus-actual review recomputed the approved scenario's predictions with the current model version, and the predicted late orders changed after the decision had been taken.

templates.title: Dangling links — target objects deleted under live links, and how long each stayed broken
templates.subtopic: interval overlap of link versions and deletion periods, outcome classification, LEFT JOIN from a dimension

sections.scenario: A manufacturer's operational applications read an ontology of objects joined by typed links (here {{link_type_list}}). Pipelines delete an object when its source row disappears, and restore it if the row comes back; applications and users re-point links to other objects or remove them. A link whose target object is deleted is dangling: applications show a broken reference until the link is fixed or the target comes back. The data quality team wants, per link type, how many dangling episodes there were, how each one ended, and how long fixes took. The tables are a snapshot taken at {{as_of}}; nothing in them happens after that time.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns link_type, episodes, removed, repointed, restored, still_dangling, avg_hours_to_fix: one row per link type in link_types (a link type with no episodes shows zeros and a NULL average), ordered by link_type. link_versions holds each link's target over time: a version is in force from valid_from (inclusive) to valid_to (exclusive), and valid_to is NULL while it is in force. Re-pointing closes version n and opens version n + 1 at the same instant with another target; removing closes the last version with no successor. object_deletions holds one row per period an object spent deleted, from deleted_at to restored_at (NULL while it is still deleted). {{restore_rule}} A dangling episode is the overlap of one link version with one deletion period of its target object: it starts at the later of valid_from and deleted_at, ends at the earlier of valid_to and restored_at (a NULL end is open), and counts only if it starts strictly before it ends. Each episode is still dangling if both ends are open; otherwise the earlier end decides how it ended: repointed if valid_to ended it and the link has a next version, removed if valid_to ended it and the link has none, restored if restored_at ended it first. When valid_to equals restored_at, credit the link change (removed or repointed). avg_hours_to_fix is the total length in seconds of the link type's resolved episodes (removed, repointed or restored) ÷ (3600 × their number), rounded to 2 decimal places. {{grace_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{versions}} link versions and {{deletions}} deletion periods; production has hundreds of millions of links. Times are UTC. Every target_object_id exists in objects.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, link types, object ids and times; the model is this exercise's, not a description of any product's internals. Only the target side matters here (deleted source objects are handled by another check). Every new version of a link changes its target.
sections.criteria: Interval overlap computed with the later start and the earlier end, open ends handled, zero-length overlaps excluded; the start taken from the version when the target was already deleted; outcomes classified by which end came first, with the tie credited to the link and "next version" decided per link; one row per link type from link_types with counts that are 0 (not 1) for clean types; the average over resolved episodes only, rounded as stated; at Hard and above, several deletion periods per object; at Very Hard, the grace period applied exactly; deterministic ordering; can explain incremental maintenance and late feeds.

clarifications.q: A link was re-pointed to an object that had already been deleted. Is that an episode?
clarifications.a: Yes, a new one. It starts when that version starts, not when the object was deleted.

clarifications.q: The target was deleted at exactly the instant the link version ended.
clarifications.a: That overlap has zero length, so it is not an episode.

clarifications.q: Two links point at the same deleted object. One episode or two?
clarifications.a: Two. Episodes belong to link versions, not to objects.

clarifications.q: Does a still-dangling episode count in the average?
clarifications.a: No. It has no end yet; it counts in episodes and still_dangling only.
